beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two whole pizzas and one quarter of another. A mixed number names wholes and an extra fraction.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: How many quarter slices is that?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Open the first pizza into four equal quarters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Open the second. Four more quarters. Eight so far.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And the extra quarter makes nine quarters!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine is the numerator: the number of pieces. Four is the denominator: four equal pieces make one whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine fourths is an improper fraction: its top number is at least its bottom number. It names one whole or more.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Go the other way. Here are twenty-two eighths. Every eight pieces make one whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Close eight into one whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Close eight more into a second whole. Two wholes use sixteen pieces.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Six eighths are left. They cannot fill another whole.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So the whole-number part is two. The fraction left over is six eighths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Pair the eighths. Each pair is a quarter. Six eighths is three quarters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Divide the piece count by the pieces per whole. Full groups give the whole part; the remainder gives the leftover pieces.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A recipe needs three and one third cups of oats. One and two thirds cups are already poured. How much more is needed?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: We need to account for one whole cup and two thirds.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One whole is easy. But I only see one third. How can I take away two thirds?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Open one full cup into three equal portions. Each is one third of a cup.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Bring those three thirds beside the extra third.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two whole cups stay. Three thirds plus one third makes four thirds.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: We did not add any oats. We just opened a whole!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two wholes and four thirds. That is another way to write the same amount.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now take away the one whole cup already poured.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And take away two of the thirds.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One whole and two thirds remain. We need one and two thirds cups more.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Keep the subtraction in order. If the first fraction is smaller, open a whole to get enough pieces.

do.text: Need more pieces? Open a whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Open every whole. Three wholes make nine thirds. One extra makes ten thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The amount already poured is one whole and two thirds. Three thirds plus two thirds makes five thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten thirds minus five thirds leaves five thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Close three of them into one whole. Two thirds remain.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Same oats, same answer. If the answer box asks for a fraction, enter five thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Lena uses three and four fifths meters of string, then one and four fifths meters more. Each long strip is one meter.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add the wholes: three plus one makes four. Add the fifths: four plus four makes eight fifths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four wholes and eight fifths. There is another whole hiding in those pieces.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Bring five fifths together. They close into exactly one meter.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Three fifths are left. Four whole meters plus the new whole makes five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: In fifths, that is five times five, plus three: twenty-eight fifths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: You could also add entirely in fifths. Nineteen fifths plus nine fifths gives twenty-eight fifths.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four fifths plus four fifths. Should I add both numbers and get eight tenths?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Watch the pieces. Joining them does not cut them smaller. They are fifths before, and fifths after.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The numerator counts pieces: eight. The denominator names their size: fifths.

do.text: Add the counts. Keep the denominator.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five fifths fill exactly one whole. Close the whole, with no pieces left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three fifths fill less than a whole. Keep the fraction.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Your turn, Champ. Four and one eighth minus two and five eighths. Which whole could you open?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One whole holds eight eighths. With the extra eighth, I will have nine.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Open it. Three wholes and nine eighths is the same amount.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Move the eighths where we can count them.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Take away two wholes, and five eighths.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One whole and four eighths. Four of eight equal pieces is half a whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And as a fraction, one and one half is three halves.

parts.label: \text{A whole is a full set of pieces.}

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A whole is a full set of equal pieces.

do.text: One amount, two ways to count it

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Open one when you need pieces.

do.text: Open a whole to get more pieces.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Close one when you have a full set.

do.text: Close a full set to make a whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The pieces move. The amount stays the same.
